title: Precision Testing Laboratories, Ltd. v. Kenyon Corporation of America
lead: Negotiations for an automobile-certification venture never became a binding joint venture, but the engineer’s valuable work still supported a limited restitution recovery.

actors.name: Asher Hiesiger and Precision Testing Laboratories
actors.role: Investor and his company asserting venture and restitution claims

actors.name: Arthur Ellis
actors.role: Texas Coach operator contributing engineering work

actors.name: Lawrence Kenyon and Kenyon Corporation of America
actors.role: Individual and corporation benefiting from certification

actors.name: Kenneth Bloom
actors.role: Kenyon’s attorney preparing proposed venture documents

proceedings: Federal district court after bench trial on liability: rejected joint-venture contract and most restitution claims; preserved Ellis’s service-based recovery against both defendants, with damages reserved.
limits: The August 26, 1986 decision contains trial findings but fixes no damages amount and grants no stock ownership or venture profits. Contributions by one participant cannot be attributed automatically to another claimant.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Separate projects bring financial, technical, and regulatory resources together
sections.cue: Introduce the participants before the proposed joint venture.
paragraphs: Asher Hiesiger, a lawyer and real-estate investor, owned Precision Testing Laboratories, or PTL. Arthur Ellis ran Texas Coach and related Houston businesses and had developed successful emissions systems. Lawrence Kenyon owned Kenyon Corporation of America, or KCA, which held small-volume-manufacturer status but initially lacked a successful certification vehicle. That status combined with a conforming prototype could permit applying an approved emissions system to similar gray-market imported cars without individually testing each one.

During 1983, Hiesiger funded an unsuccessful Porsche project with Kenyon, obtained Mercedes testing time, and let Kenyon occupy a Manhattan apartment rent free. Independently, he paid Ellis for research and a Porsche conversion. Engineer Claus Liphardt developed components underlying the later Mercedes system; the court did not credit Kenyon with originating that engineering. A December meeting mainly arranged an information exchange between Ellis and Kenyon in Houston, not a concluded three-way agreement.

In January 1984, Ellis and Kenyon tested components and discussed collaboration, including a possible half-interest in KCA for Ellis. Ellis chose a different catalytic converter, developed a no-air-pump configuration, investigated the fuel block, and reengineered the regulator. Hiesiger privately advanced Ellis $100,000. A separate letter pledged assets including Ellis’s anticipated KCA interest, unknown to Kenyon. Those transfers therefore did not automatically establish performance of a shared venture.

sections.title: February discussions leave ownership and control unfinished
sections.cue: Trace the alleged agreement and continued work.
paragraphs: Plaintiffs claimed a binding venture arose February 17. Trial testimony and Kenyon’s contemporaneous notes supported discussion of a fifty-twenty-five-twenty-five stock division, each plaintiff paying $5,000 for a quarter interest. At least fifteen proposals addressed inventory, components, a parts-finder fee, cars belonging to Kenyon’s mother, housing, and a separate Gelaendewagen business. Some were accepted, but liabilities and other matters remained disputed.

Kenyon and Hiesiger called attorney Kenneth Bloom about formal documents; Ellis did not participate in that call. Kenyon and Bloom said commitment required writing and counsel’s approval. Hiesiger called the papers a memorial, yet asked counsel to solve the deadlock risk in the proposed ownership split. The court found a framework for continued dealings rather than a final bargain.

Ellis nevertheless supplied substantial performance. His technicians spent ninety-three hours preparing a coast-down test, and he spent five weeks at the Ohio Automotive Testing Laboratory, sometimes working eighteen-hour days. Independent laboratory evidence supported findings that he attended more often than Kenyon, performed most physical work, and supplied the decisive intellectual contribution. KCA paid laboratory bills. The car reached certification levels April 13, followed by documentation work.

sections.title: Further drafts expose unresolved material terms
sections.cue: Follow the negotiations into the liability trial.
paragraphs: May proposals shifted shares to fifty-one, twenty-four-and-a-half, and twenty-four-and-a-half percent, contemplated $175,000 financing, gave Kenyon board control, and compensated his daily management. Plaintiffs objected. Ownership, management, salary, financing, and transfer restrictions remained open. A $10,000 check delivered in June was never negotiated; Hiesiger stopped payment, and counsel returned it denying agreement. Suit followed in July. KCA obtained conformity certificates in August 1984 and January 1985, while a competing company owned by Hiesiger’s wife separately obtained certification with Ellis’s help.

Judge Irving Ben Cooper tried liability February 10–14, reserving damages. He credited Ellis most, found much Hiesiger testimony and some Kenyon testimony unconvincing, and rejected the unsupported attempt to dismiss Kenyon individually. The record supported causes of action against both defendants.

sections.title: The evidence shows intended commitment only after formal execution
sections.cue: Explain both independent defects in the claimed venture.
paragraphs: New York allowed oral contracts but respected an expressed reservation to await formal execution. Cooper balanced reserved commitment, completeness, complexity, and partial performance without making any factor universally decisive.

Counsel was to solve open problems rather than merely transcribe a complete bargain. Even Ellis later said there had never been a three-party deal and explored working with Kenyon alone. Shares, deadlock, liabilities, and risk remained unsettled. The substantial project combined stock acquisition, financing, supplies, technical work, and an ongoing import business, requiring six proposed documents exceeding twenty-five pages.

Ellis’s engineering and inventory sales reflected some performance, but much contemplated performance never happened. An unnegotiated check did not complete stock purchase, alleged financing and administration lacked persuasive proof, and earlier laboratory access and apartment use preceded the claimed venture. On balance, no intent to bind before execution was established.

Independently, a New York joint venture needed intent, contributions, agreed profit-and-loss sharing, and joint control. The parties intended an association once formalized and proposed sufficient contributions, but never settled financial allocation or management. Contemplated shares alone did not establish joint control. Collaboration therefore did not create the asserted fiduciary venture.

sections.title: Restitution follows the particular person’s uncompensated benefit
sections.cue: Separate Ellis’s work from Hiesiger’s financial dealings.
paragraphs: Unjust enrichment remained possible despite failed formation. Ellis’s staff and prolonged engineering were essential to KCA’s certification, and defendants received that benefit without paying its principal contributor. Ellis’s ability to use what he learned elsewhere did not erase the labor directed to KCA’s success. The court distinguished Songbird, involving ordinary negotiating and self-protective resale activity rather than services intended to benefit the defendant.

Hiesiger’s claims failed for different evidentiary reasons. His private $100,000 advance was not shown to finance KCA rather than independent projects, and he himself denied it was a venture obligation. PTL’s $15,055.41 parts payment benefited Ellis’s Texas Coach. The apartment benefited Kenyon, but existing arrangements prevented Hiesiger accepting rent, so the court found no corresponding expense to him. Enrichment at the particular claimant’s expense had to be proved rather than inferred from participation.

sections.title: Only Ellis’s limited recovery remains for agreement or a damages trial
paragraphs: On August 26, 1986, Cooper dismissed the complaint except Ellis’s right to recover from both defendants the portion of money earned by his services certifying KCA’s test car. The parties were to attempt agreement on reasonable damages and submit a proposed judgment. If unable to agree within sixty days after filing of the opinion, they were to notify the court for a damages trial limited to Ellis and those services.

No amount was awarded, and no plaintiff received the proposed ownership or venture profits. The decision distinguished nonbinding negotiations from the separate injustice of retaining proved, uncompensated services.
